January WTI crude oil futures recovered from a three-month low this week as renewed concern over Middle East supply brought buyers back into the market. Prices had fallen early in the week as traders focused on the prospect of a global surplus. The selling slowed after WTI reached $79.07, and the market rallied Wednesday after Yemen’s Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery.

At 00:09 GMT Thursday, January WTI crude oil futures were trading at $84.01, up $0.60 or 0.72% for the week. The contract had traded as high as $84.27. The weekly figures are still developing ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The rally came as traders also assessed a smaller-than-expected build in U.S. crude inventories. Attention now turns to the November 29 OPEC+ meeting, where ministers are scheduled to discuss production policy for 2027.

The Houthis said Wednesday that they had attacked the Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh’s financial district. Ras Tanura is Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery and is part of a complex that also serves as a major crude export terminal.

PVM analyst Tamas Varga said the Houthi statement triggered the rally as traders added a geopolitical risk premium. He also said traders were likely covering short positions ahead of Thanksgiving.

The rally came as traders also assessed a smaller-than-expected build in U.S. crude inventories. Attention now turns to the November 29 OPEC+ meeting, where ministers are scheduled to discuss production policy for 2027.

The Houthis said Wednesday that they had attacked the Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh’s financial district. Ras Tanura is Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery and is part of a complex that also serves as a major crude export terminal.

PVM analyst Tamas Varga said the Houthi statement triggered the rally as traders added a geopolitical risk premium. He also said traders were likely covering short positions ahead of Thanksgiving.

The claim gave traders a reason to reconsider how much supply risk had been removed from prices during the recent decline. It did not establish that production or exports had been lost. The market will need more information about the attack and its impact before traders can determine whether fewer Saudi barrels are reaching buyers.

The refinery claim followed attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz. Three ships were struck by unidentified projectiles on Monday as they sailed east through the strait, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

On Tuesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said a container ship was targeted and came to a stop near the strait while sailing an unauthorized route, according to Iranian state media.

The attacks kept the threat to shipping in front of traders, but oil still fell to a three-month low this week. More crude has been reaching the market, and that has made it harder for buyers to sustain a risk premium. A disruption that removes a significant amount of oil for an extended period would give them a stronger argument.

U.S. Crude Build Falls Short of Forecast

The Energy Information Administration reported that U.S. crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20. Analysts in a Reuters poll had expected a build of about 1.5 million barrels.

Price Futures Group analyst Phil Flynn said the report helped push prices higher because traders had expected a larger increase. The smaller build arrived as the market was also reacting to the Houthi claim.

Inventories are still rising. The latest increase followed a 3.4 million-barrel build the previous week. Sellers can point to those reports as evidence that barrels are accumulating, while buyers can argue that the latest increase was not as large as feared.

Libya’s Sharara oil pipeline has also reopened after a brief halt. The National Oil Corporation said an unlawful group had closed a valve on the line. Its reopening adds to the oil reaching the market just as traders are weighing the risk of a disruption elsewhere.

OPEC+ ministers are scheduled to meet on November 29 to discuss 2027 output policy. Their decision comes with the International Energy Agency forecasting a return to a global surplus and a potentially larger surplus next year.

Iraq and Kazakhstan are pressing for higher estimates of their production capacity, according to people familiar with the matter. The estimates are part of a review that will help determine how much members can pump in 2027. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the review is expected to be completed by year-end.

The United Arab Emirates is no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies, according to LSEG oil research specialist Zhenqiang Seto. That adds another question for traders trying to determine how much supply could reach the market next year.

For now, Wednesday’s rally shows that traders are not ready to dismiss the threat to Middle East supply. The OPEC+ meeting will test the other side of the market: whether producers are prepared to add more oil while inventories are building and the IEA is forecasting a surplus.
